subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: Two days before the inter-house quiz, the hall still wasn't booked and the corridor had no posters. Pradeep, the house captain, sat on the stairs with his list and talked it through under his breath. "If I do the posters, they'll look like a spider walked through ink. Samir's notebook headings are neater than printed ones, so posters are his." He crossed out his own name. "The hall slip is harder. I go blank in front of the office clerks. But the vice-captain runs errands there every lunch break and knows everyone by name. They'll say yes to a familiar face." He texted both of them before the bell. By Thursday afternoon Samir had three bright posters on the notice board, and the vice-captain came back waving a signed slip. The hall was theirs for Friday.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep give the posters to Samir?
qa.a: Because Samir's notebook headings are neater than printed ones.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling about going to the office himself?
qa.a: Pradeep felt nervous about it; he says he goes blank in front of the office clerks, which is part of why he hands the slip to someone at ease there.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep have tried if nobody on the team knew the office staff?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher in charge of the quiz to introduce them, or take a short written request so his nerves matter less.

qa.q: How might Samir see being picked for the posters?
qa.a: Samir would likely feel pleased and trusted, because he was chosen for a skill he actually has rather than handed a random job.

grounding: A teen captain, short on time, reasons aloud about who suits each job: neat lettering for posters, familiarity with the office for the permission.

subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: On the metro home, Dilnaz scrolled through the class group and talked her plan out loud to Divyansh. "The book swap needs posters by Monday and a yes for the courtyard. I was going to split jobs alphabetically, but that's silly." She tapped the screen. "The boy who does calligraphy for the school magazine: his letters are gorgeous, so posters go to him. And you." She pointed at Divyansh. "You're on first-name terms with half the office because of debate club. You ask for the courtyard." Divyansh grinned. "So I'm the talker?" "You're the one they'll say yes to. If I send someone they've never met, it waits a week." He agreed before their station. On Monday the posters went up, and the courtyard was booked for Saturday morning.

qa.q: What event is Dilnaz's class planning?
qa.a: A book swap, which needs posters by Monday and a yes for the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz drop her first idea of splitting jobs alphabetically?
qa.a: She realised it was silly and felt uneasy about the delay a stranger might face; matching jobs to what people are good at felt more sensible and hopeful.

qa.q: Which other approach could work if Divyansh were busy with exams?
qa.a: Dilnaz could go with a teacher who knows the office, or ask Divyansh for a quick introduction so the request still comes through a familiar face.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see being chosen as 'the talker'?
qa.a: He seems amused and a little flattered that his debate-club friendships are useful, and he agrees quickly.

grounding: A student captain explains aloud why the calligraphy student gets the posters and the well-connected classmate gets the permission.

subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]
passage:
Subject: Survey data, over to you

Hi Wasim,

Thanks for taking the cleaning off my plate. Here's what the final sheet needs to look like:

1. One row per respondent. Delete the 14 test entries from the first day (they're marked TEST).
2. Ages as plain numbers, so "19 yrs" becomes 19.
3. Blank answers stay blank. Please don't fill them with zero.
4. Keep the raw file untouched and work on a copy.

Could you send me the first 30 cleaned rows by Wednesday at 6 pm? I'll look at them that evening, and if the format is right you can carry on with the rest at your own pace until the Sunday deadline. If anything in the raw file confuses you, message me before guessing. I'd much rather answer five small questions than fix one big surprise.

Thanks,
Lokesh

qa.q: How many test entries does Wasim need to delete?
qa.a: 14 test entries from the first day, marked TEST.

qa.q: What does the line 'message me before guessing' suggest Lokesh is worried about?
qa.a: Lokesh is worried about quiet guesses turning into big mistakes later, and wants Wasim to feel free to ask rather than anxious about bothering anyone.

qa.q: What else could Lokesh add to make the handover even clearer?
qa.a: Attaching one already cleaned example row would show the format at a glance, so Wasim has less to interpret.

qa.q: How might the email feel to Wasim?
qa.a: Wasim probably feels trusted and clear about what 'done' means, with a safe check on Wednesday to catch errors before the Sunday deadline.

grounding: A student lead hands over data cleaning with a clear format and a Wednesday check on a small sample.

subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]
passage: So, I'm Tushar, and last term I finally learnt how to hand work over properly. Our civil engineering group had traffic counts from four junctions, typed by four different people. Total mess. Indu offered to clean it. Earlier I'd have said "just sort it", then lain awake wondering what she was doing. This time I sat with her for ten minutes. I showed her exactly what I needed: times in 24-hour format, one junction per tab, and vehicle types spelt the same way every time, "two-wheeler", never "bike" or "scooty". Then I said, "Don't spend more than an hour before you show me. Send me Junction B by Wednesday lunch." She sent it Wednesday at noon, and there was one problem: she'd merged buses and vans. We fixed it in five minutes, not five days.

qa.q: Which junction did Indu send first, and when?
qa.a: Junction B, on Wednesday at noon.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel about handing over work in the past?
qa.a: Tushar felt anxious and out of control, lying awake wondering what the other person was doing after just saying "just sort it".

qa.q: What would you change first if the group had missed the Wednesday check?
qa.a: Set a new short check straight away on one small piece, so a mistake like merging buses and vans is still caught early.

qa.q: What is it like for Indu to get such clear instructions?
qa.a: Indu can work confidently without guessing, and the early check means her one mistake was cheap to fix rather than embarrassing at the end.

grounding: A student lead explains the format for cleaning traffic data and agrees on a sample by Wednesday lunch.

subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]
passage: Aiko had been team lead at the Rotterdam shipping office for three weeks when she handed Emil the quarterly supplier report. "Take it end to end," she said. "I trust you." On Thursday evening his draft arrived. It was solid, just ordered differently from how she would have done it. At eleven that night she was still at her kitchen table, moving every section, changing his charts, rewording his summary. She sent the new version to the client at 8 a.m. with her name first. At stand-up, Emil scrolled through the file history and went quiet. He didn't offer to take the next report. By Friday Aiko had two reports of her own on her desk, a stiff neck, and a colleague who answered her in single words.

qa.q: What time was Aiko still working on the report?
qa.a: At eleven that night she was still at her kitchen table.

qa.q: What does Emil going quiet at stand-up suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and distrusted: his solid draft had been rewritten without a word to him, despite "I trust you".

qa.q: What could Aiko do differently with the next report?
qa.a: She could agree up front on the structure she wants, then give Emil notes to fix his own draft instead of rewriting it.

qa.q: How does the situation look from the client's side?
qa.a: The client only sees one report, but if Emil pulls back, the team slows down and Aiko becomes a bottleneck for every future piece.

grounding: A new lead delegates a report, then rewrites it overnight, leaving the colleague distrusted and herself with twice the work.

subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]
passage: At the community centre, Aadhya had been programme lead for a month. The grant progress report was due in ten days, so she asked Anirban to draft it; he had run the evening classes all year and knew the numbers. His draft landed on Tuesday. It told the story through two learners, where Aadhya would have used tables. That weekend she rewrote it from the first line. On Monday Anirban opened the shared folder, saw his name gone from the file, and closed the laptop without a word. After that he stopped suggesting ideas in meetings. Meanwhile Aadhya's own budget sheet, the thing only she could do, slid past its deadline. The funder got a neat report. The centre got a quieter Anirban and a lead running on four hours' sleep.

qa.q: When did Anirban's draft arrive?
qa.a: His draft landed on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he closed the laptop without a word?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and pushed aside, since his work and his name had been removed from the file.

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Aadhya better?
qa.a: Telling Anirban at the start that the funder likes tables, then letting him adjust his own draft, would keep his effort and her time.

qa.q: How do the learners at the centre get affected by this?
qa.a: With Anirban withdrawing and Aadhya exhausted, fewer new ideas reach the classes and planning slows.

grounding: A new lead delegates a grant report, rewrites it entirely, and the colleague withdraws while her own work slips.

subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]
passage: Come, sit, Alka. You asked how your Damini Aunty learnt to run a team. I'll tell you. I was twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift, and I checked every label the junior pharmacist printed. Every single one. By the third week I was falling asleep standing, and the junior had stopped asking me anything. One night I noticed the junior had spotted a wrong dose on a doctor's slip and said nothing, waiting for me to find it. That frightened me more than any mistake. The next evening I said, "Here is what a good shift looks like: every order checked against the chart, doubts flagged to me, the log complete by six." How to get there, I left to the junior. At the end of each week we looked at the log together. Within a month the log was cleaner than mine.

qa.q: How old was Damini's younger self when put in charge of the night shift?
qa.a: Twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift.

qa.q: Why was young Damini frightened on the night the junior stayed silent?
qa.a: Seeing the junior spot a wrong dose and stay silent, waiting; it frightened the young lead because checking everything had taught the junior not to speak up.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Stating what a good shift looks like and leaving the method to the junior; clear standards plus weekly feedback built skill and trust instead of dependence.

qa.q: How might the junior pharmacist have felt once the lead stopped rechecking every label?
qa.a: Probably trusted and more responsible, which is why the junior's log soon became cleaner than the lead's.

grounding: An elder recalls moving from checking everything to stating the outcome, stepping back and giving weekly feedback, which raised quality and trust.

subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]
passage: Raghav had a problem: the client dashboard was due Friday, and he would be on a site visit in the hills all week with one bar of signal. On his last project he had hovered over Harish's shoulder, changing fonts and filters, and both of them had been miserable. This time there was no chance to hover. On Monday morning he wrote three lines on the whiteboard: "The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance. It must load in under five seconds. Numbers must match the finance sheet." He turned to Harish. "How you build it is up to you." On Thursday night, from a guesthouse, he opened Harish's link. It was not how he'd have done it; it was simpler. He sent two notes on the colour labels and one "This is really clear." The client signed off on Friday.

qa.q: What three things did Raghav write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance, it must load in under five seconds, and the numbers must match the finance sheet.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when he saw Harish's version was not how he'd have done it?
qa.a: Raghav may have felt a flicker of unease, but he felt reassured that it was simpler and met the goals, and chose to praise it rather than redo it.

qa.q: What else could Raghav try if he had good signal and was tempted to hover again?
qa.a: He could still fix a single midweek check-in instead of watching every step, so Harish keeps ownership of the method.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish on this project compared with the last one?
qa.a: Harish gets room to choose the method and clear, specific feedback, instead of constant changes, so the work feels his own.

grounding: A lead facing a constraint states the outcome, leaves the method to the colleague and gives brief feedback, improving the result and trust.

subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]
passage:
Note for the crèche, Tuesday

This morning Jyoti sat with her little jar of shape blocks and pulled at the lid until her face went red. Then she stopped, walked over, and pushed the jar into my lap with a small whimper: "Mama, Mama." I loosened it a little and handed it back so she could finish opening it herself. She did, and clapped 🙂 She may bring you stuck things today as well.

Vandana

qa.q: What did Jyoti push into the writer's lap?
qa.a: Her little jar of shape blocks, with a small whimper.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling before she walked over to the writer?
qa.a: She was frustrated: she pulled until her face went red before giving up and asking for help.

qa.q: What does the writer's approach do well?
qa.a: Loosening the lid a little and handing it back lets Jyoti finish the job herself, so she feels proud of her effort and also learns that asking helps.

qa.q: How might a crèche teacher use this note during the day?
qa.a: The teacher can expect Jyoti to bring stuck things over and can respond the same way, helping a little rather than doing it all.

grounding: A toddler who cannot open a lid brings the jar to her mother with a whimper, using the caregiver as a helper.

subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]
passage: In the courtyard, Amma sat sorting rice. Mahima, not yet two, had the little wooden box her big brother Divyansh had made her. The sliding lid was stuck. She pushed with both thumbs, then banged it on the floor. Her lip wobbled. She toddled over, leaned on Amma's knee and held the box up, whimpering. Amma eased the lid back a finger's width. Mahima slid it open and shook out three tamarind seeds.

qa.q: What did Divyansh make for Mahima?
qa.a: A small wooden box with a sliding lid.

qa.q: How can you tell Mahima was upset before she went to Amma?
qa.a: She banged the box and her lip wobbled; she was frustrated and close to tears when nothing worked.

qa.q: What could Amma try next time to help Mahima learn?
qa.a: She could show Mahima slowly how to push the lid sideways with her thumb, so next time Mahima might manage it alone.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel if he saw the lid stick?
qa.a: He might feel a bit sorry that his gift was hard to open and want to sand the lid so it slides easily.

grounding: A toddler holds a stuck toy up to her mother, whimpering, using the caregiver to solve what she cannot.

subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]
passage: Xin's new trainers had real laces, like the ones his friend Yosef tied all by himself. At the door, Xin tugged the loops into a knot that fell apart twice. He sat on the step, then looked up. "Yeye, can you show me? Slowly?" Grandpa knelt down. "Watch. Bunny ear, then round the tree, then through the hole." He did it once, very slowly. Then he put his big warm hands over Xin's small ones and they made the bunny ear together. The first bow was lopsided. The second one held all the way to the park.

qa.q: What did Xin ask Yeye?
qa.a: "Yeye, can you show me? Slowly?"

qa.q: Why did Xin want to learn to tie his laces?
qa.a: He wanted to be like his friend Yosef, and he felt frustrated when his knot kept falling apart; he hoped Yeye's help would fix it.

qa.q: What small step helped Xin most?
qa.a: Grandpa's hands guiding his made the steps easy to feel; next time Xin could try alone while Grandpa just watches.

qa.q: How might Yeye feel being asked for help?
qa.a: Yeye probably felt pleased and patient, glad that Xin trusted him enough to ask.

grounding: A child who cannot tie laces asks his grandfather to show him, watches slowly, then ties with the grandfather's hands guiding his.

subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]
passage: After swimming class at the sports club, Ojas pulled on his school shoes and stared at the flapping laces. Tejas, from his class, was already out of the door. Ojas carried his shoe to the bench where Dadu waited. "Dadu, teach me the loops. Tejas can do it." Dadu set the shoe on his knee. "Look carefully." He made one loop, wrapped the other lace round it and pulled, very slowly. "Now you." It flopped open. Dadu covered Ojas's fingers with his own. "Together." Round, through, pull. Ojas grinned at the bow.

qa.q: Where was Dadu waiting?
qa.a: On the bench, where Ojas carried his shoe after swimming class.

qa.q: What might Ojas be feeling when Tejas was already out of the door?
qa.a: He probably felt a little left behind and embarrassed that he couldn't tie his laces yet, which pushed him to ask Dadu.

qa.q: What would you advise Ojas's teacher at the club if other children need the same help?
qa.a: Show the loops slowly once, then guide each child's hands, the same way Dadu did, before letting them try alone.

qa.q: How does Dadu see Ojas's request?
qa.a: Dadu seems happy to be asked and takes it seriously, slowing down so Ojas can actually learn.

grounding: A young child asks his grandfather a direct question about laces, watches, then practises with the grandfather's hands guiding.

subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Avni spent twenty minutes on question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations. She tried drawing the tracks, rubbed it out, tried a table. Her eraser left a hole in the page. "Okay," she whispered. "I've tried three ways. Now I need someone to see what I did, not just give me the answer."

Tuesday: Before assembly she took her messy page to Reena Ma'am. "I think I went wrong somewhere here," Avni said, pointing. "I added their speeds, but maybe I should have subtracted?" Reena Ma'am smiled. "What made you unsure?" Avni thought. "They're going the same way, so they're not coming closer fast."

Thursday: In the quiz, a similar question came up. Avni didn't panic. She drew the arrows first.

qa.q: Which question did Avni spend twenty minutes on?
qa.a: Question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations.

qa.q: How did Avni feel on Thursday when a similar question came up?
qa.a: She felt calm and confident; she didn't panic because she now understood why the direction of the trains mattered.

qa.q: Why did bringing her messy page to Reena Ma'am work well?
qa.a: Reena Ma'am could see exactly where Avni's thinking went wrong and ask a question, so Avni found the fix herself.

qa.q: What would change if Avni had only asked for the answer?
qa.a: She might have copied it without knowing why, and the Thursday quiz question could have caught her out again.

grounding: A girl works a maths problem alone, then brings her attempt to the teacher so the teacher can see where her thinking went wrong.

subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]
passage: Shreya, you think I was always good at sums? No. When I was a girl of eleven, there was a problem about filling a tank with two taps. I sat with it for a whole evening. I tried one way, then another. My pages were full of crossings. My brother said, "Just ask Master-ji for the answer." But I thought, if I only get the answer, I will be stuck again next week. So I took my crossed-out pages to school. I told Master-ji, "This is how I thought. Somewhere it breaks." He read my pages and put his finger on one line. "Here, you forgot one tap was emptying." I nearly laughed. The next tank problem, I solved alone. That's how your Pooja Nani learnt.

qa.q: What was the problem young Pooja struggled with?
qa.a: A problem about filling a tank with two taps.

qa.q: Why did young Pooja refuse to just ask for the answer?
qa.a: She was worried that with only the answer she would be stuck again next week; she wanted to understand where her own thinking broke.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Taking her crossed-out pages to Master-ji; seeing her working let him point to the exact line where she forgot one tap was emptying.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt reading her pages?
qa.a: He was probably pleased and impressed to see a student who had really tried, which made it easy for him to help quickly.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a girl, trying a maths problem for an evening and taking her own attempt to the teacher to find the flaw.

subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]
passage: I'm Karthik, final year, and I want to tell you about the most useful coffee I ever had. I was stuck between physiotherapy and sports science, so I messaged an alumna, Vandana, who runs a clinic now. Before meeting her, I sat down and wrote exactly three questions. One: what skills matter most in her first two years? Two: which entry path would she pick today, the master's or a clinic job straight away? Three: what does a normal Tuesday look like for her? At the café I put my notebook on the table and wrote while she talked. She laughed and said most students just ask, "Is it a good career?" That evening I made two columns in my notebook and compared her answers with what my professor had told me.

qa.q: How many questions did Karthik write before the meeting?
qa.a: Exactly three questions.

qa.q: How do you think Karthik felt going into the meeting?
qa.a: Karthik likely felt a little nervous but prepared and focused, since the questions were written and ready in the notebook.

qa.q: What else could Karthik do to get a fuller picture?
qa.a: Speak to one more person on the other path, sports science, with the same three questions, so the comparison is fair.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Karthik's approach?
qa.a: She seems amused and pleased; she laughs because most students only ask "Is it a good career?"

grounding: A student planning a career meets an alumna with three written questions and takes notes to compare later.

subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]
passage: My name's Jatin. I share a room with Aadhya at the hostel, and I watched how she got ready to meet the alumnus who works as an urban planner. The night before, she wasn't scrolling. She was writing on an index card, crossing out, rewriting. When I peeked, I saw three questions: skills to learn now, how people actually get their first job, and what a working day is like. In the morning she ironed a kurta, then read the card again on the bus. When she came back she had two pages of notes, underlined in two colours. She didn't say much about how it went. She just pinned the pages above her desk, next to her placement list, and started marking things off.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya write her questions?
qa.a: On an index card, the night before.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have been feeling, judging from the cues Jatin describes?
qa.a: She seemed serious and perhaps a bit nervous, rewriting her card and reading it again on the bus; she also seems determined afterwards.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try next time to get even more from such a meeting?
qa.a: She could send her three questions ahead, so the alumnus can think about them and give fuller answers.

qa.q: How might the alumnus see Aadhya's preparation?
qa.a: The alumnus would likely feel respected and find it easier to help, because her questions were clear and specific.

grounding: An observer describes a student preparing three questions for a professional and taking notes to compare later.

subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]
passage:
Week 1: At the start-up meet, Irfan, a mentor who advises café owners in the big city, looked at Aparna's price list for her home-baked cakes. "Too cheap," he said. "Double everything. People pay for premium." Aparna nodded and wrote it down. She didn't ask why.

Week 3: She printed new cards with the doubled prices. Her regulars in the small town, mostly teachers and shop owners ordering for birthdays, went quiet. Only two orders came that week instead of the usual nine.

Week 5: A neighbour said gently, "Beta, we loved your cakes, but this is city money." Aparna sat with the order book and realised Irfan's clients were office crowds in the city, not her street. She had never asked what his advice was based on.

qa.q: How many orders came in week 3, compared with usual?
qa.a: Only two orders instead of the usual nine.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she sat with the order book in week 5?
qa.a: She probably felt dismayed and a bit foolish, realising she had followed Irfan's advice without asking what it was based on.

qa.q: What could Aparna have asked Irfan in week 1?
qa.a: She could have asked why he suggested doubling, and who his clients were, then tested one new price with a few regulars before changing everything.

qa.q: How did the change look to Aparna's regular customers?
qa.a: To her regulars it felt like the cakes were suddenly priced for the city, not for them, so they quietly stopped ordering.

grounding: A young entrepreneur follows an adviser's pricing tip without asking why and misses that his market differs from hers.

subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]
passage: Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, before this workshop had a sign board. I made hand-stitched cushion covers, and I found an adviser, Francis, who had helped big wholesale sellers. He said, "Cut your price in half. Win on volume." He sounded so sure, and I was so eager, I didn't ask a single question. I cut my prices. But my buyers were small boutiques. They saw the new price and thought the quality had dropped. Two stopped ordering. One owner told me, "At that price, it can't be handwork." Francis wasn't wrong for his world. His world was different from mine. Remember that, when you start: Binita Aunty learnt it the costly way.

qa.q: What did Francis tell young Binita to do?
qa.a: "Cut your price in half. Win on volume."

qa.q: Why didn't young Binita question Francis's advice?
qa.a: She was eager and he sounded so sure, so she felt too impressed and hurried to ask why.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Binita have made a better choice?
qa.a: When Francis gave the advice; asking what kind of sellers he had helped would have shown his wholesale world differed from her boutique buyers.

qa.q: How did the boutique owners see the lower prices?
qa.a: They took the cheaper price as a sign the quality had dropped, and one said it couldn't be handwork at that price.

grounding: An elder recalls following an adviser's pricing advice without asking why and missing that his market differed from hers.

subtype: Approach: asks for the reasoning and checks it against a second source [Revision]
passage:
Incubator mentor's note, week 6

Ira came to me after her session with Thomas, the pricing adviser. He had suggested she move her tutoring service to a monthly subscription. Instead of just nodding, she asked him why. He explained it worked for his clients because their families paid in advance. Ira then called a second practitioner, someone who runs a small tutoring centre locally, who said many parents here prefer paying per term, not per month. Ira brought both answers to me today. She has decided on a term plan with a small trial month for new families, a mix of both views fitted to her own parents. I suggested she ask ten current families before launching. She agreed and left with a question list.

qa.q: What did Thomas suggest to Ira?
qa.a: He suggested she move her tutoring service to a monthly subscription.

qa.q: What does Ira asking 'why' suggest about how she felt about the advice?
qa.a: She seems cautious and curious rather than doubtful; she wanted to feel sure the advice fitted her own families before acting.

qa.q: What else could Ira do before launching the term plan?
qa.a: Ask ten current families, as the mentor suggested, or run the trial month with a few families first and adjust.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Ira's decision to mix his idea with another?
qa.a: He might feel respected that she asked for his reasons, even if she didn't copy his plan exactly.

grounding: She asks the adviser for the reasoning, checks with a second practitioner and adapts the advice to her own customers.

subtype: Approach: asks for the reasoning and checks it against a second source [Revision]
passage:
Thursday night

Long day. At the market stall this morning I kept thinking about what the design adviser told me last week: "Switch all your pottery to matte glaze, it sells better." A week ago I would have just done it. Today I actually rang and asked why. Answer: in the city galleries, buyers want a modern look. Fair. But my buyers are tourists and local families who pick up mugs to use every day. So after lunch I called Payal, who has made pottery near the lake for years. She said matte shows tea stains faster, and her customers complain. Interesting! So here's my plan: matte for the decorative bowls, glossy for everyday mugs. I'll put six of each on the stall on Sunday and see what goes. Feeling clearer than I have all month. Manjula, you're learning.

qa.q: Who did Manjula call after lunch?
qa.a: Payal, who has made pottery near the lake for years.

qa.q: How is Manjula feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Manjula feels clearer and more confident than all month, even a little proud: "Manjula, you're learning."
